method: Web search for carpet pile heights, pile compression under foot-like pressure, friction of rubber-type soles on carpet, rolling resistance on carpet and published carpet contact parameters, preferring standards, papers and manufacturer pages. Every value below was read from the fetched page or PDF (scanned PDFs were rendered to images and read page by page). Derived values state their rule. Values that rest on one source carry single_source: true. The repository and its branches were searched for the robot_floor carpet (git grep over every branch tip); its definition is recorded verbatim. The survey started 2026-11-07 and ended shortly after midnight UTC; every source was fetched on 2026-11-07.
units: Lengths in mm, pressures in kPa, friction coefficients dimensionless, stiffness per unit area in kPa/mm, unless a key says otherwise.

mujoco_modeling.title: MuJoCo documentation, Modeling: Solver parameters and contact parameter mixing
mujoco_modeling.verification: Page fetched. b = 2 / (d_w timeconst); k = d(r) / (d_w^2 timeconst^2 dampratio^2); negative solref = (-stiffness, -damping) with b = damping / d_w, k = stiffness d(r) / d_w^2; solimp (d_0, d_w, width, midpoint, power); a higher-priority geom's solref, solimp and friction are used.

mujoco_computation.title: MuJoCo documentation, Computation: soft constraints
mujoco_computation.verification: Page fetched. Eq. (12): R_ii = (1 - d_i) / d_i * A_hat_ii, where A_hat approximates diag(J M^-1 J^T) from the 'end-effector' inertias at qpos0. Eq. (13): a_ref = -b (Jv) - k r. Also checked numerically in MuJoCo 3.10.0 (tests/test_carpet.py): efc_diagA equals body_invweight0[body, 0] for a contact with the world, and the settled depth of a free box matches the closed form to machine precision.

'In the nominal standing trials the deepest sole contacts were 0.16 mm and 2.67 mm respectively.' 'This represents level, dry, bonded low-pile material on a rigid subfloor.' 'No coefficients have yet been fitted to specimens.' 'On carpet, peak tilt reaches 18.3° and 18.2° during the corresponding holds.'

robot_floor_definition.docstring: Uniform contact-material surrogates for the intermediate robot. These are calibration hypotheses for a dry rigid indoor floor and low pile bonded to a rigid subfloor. They do not represent pile direction, snagging, seams or loose rugs. Use an actual force/indentation and slip test to fit both.
robot_floor_definition.parameter_semantics: friction = sliding coefficient, torsional length (m), rolling length (m). solref = time constant (s), damping ratio. solimp width is in metres.
robot_floor_definition.apply_surface: Sets the floor geom's priority to one above every other geom (so its parameters win), condim 6, and the solref, solimp and friction of the named surface. Refuses models with explicit floor contact pairs.
robot_floor_definition.basis: model values; no source or specimen fit is given in the repository
robot_floor_definition.note: With a positive (time-constant) solref, MuJoCo scales the contact stiffness by the effective mass of the contacting body, so the same solref gives a different stiffness in N/m on every robot, and a free body's static depth does not depend on its weight. A fixed solref is therefore not a fixed physical carpet (shown numerically in tests/test_carpet.py).

low.note: flooringclarity_2025 gives low/commercial 0.08-0.2 in (2.0-5.1 mm), inside this band

high.note: flooringclarity_2025 calls 0.4-0.75 in plush/frieze and treats shag (0.75-1.5 in+) separately; shag is outside this screen

measured_samples_mm.hirai_gunji_2001: pile length 3.5-7.0 mm, total thickness 5.0-11.0 mm (seven nylon tile, rug and mat carpets, Table 1)
measured_samples_mm.vuruskan_2017: 7, 11 and 16 mm (Wilton acrylic cut pile, Table 2)
measured_samples_mm.daulta_varshney_2021: 10, 12 and 14 mm (hand-tufted 80/20 wool-nylon cut pile, Table 1)

pile_height.verification: The two web guides agree on the medium band and on 3/4 in as the top of high pile. The measured research samples fall inside the low, medium and high bands.

hirai_gunji_2001_98kPa.method: Compressive elasticity tester B10-8001 (Matsui), JIS L 1022-1992 'Testing methods for loss of thickness by loading of textile floor covering', Method 6. Initial load 1.96 kPa, final load 98 kPa held 5 min, specimen 5 cm x 5 cm, dry. Table 3 lists the loads as 0.2 N and 9.8 N, which implies a presser foot of about 1 cm2 (derived).
hirai_gunji_2001_98kPa.definition: Compressibility (%) = (t0 - t1) / t0 x 100, with t0 the thickness under the initial load and t1 after 5 min under the final load; compressive elasticity modulus (%) = (t0' - t1) / (t0 - t1) x 100, with t0' the thickness after removing the final load.
hirai_gunji_2001_98kPa.derivation: compression = compressibility x t0, taking t0 as the Table 1 thickness; fraction = compression / pile length. Backing compression is included, so the fraction can overstate pile compression (sample E has a non-woven backing).
hirai_gunji_2001_98kPa.verification: Transcribed from the rendered Table 1 and Table 3 images; derived values recomputed by tests/test_carpet.py.

iso_3415_1986_example.note: A worked example of the calculation in the standard, not a property of a named carpet. 220 kPa is held for 2 h, so it includes creep.

daulta_varshney_2021_200kPa.method: BS 4908 (equivalent to ISO 2094 per the authors); thickness at 2 kPa, loads 2-200 kPa, recovery back to 2 kPa; WIRA digital thickness gauge.
daulta_varshney_2021_200kPa.definitions: TR (%) = Tr / T2 x 100; CR (%) = (Tr - T200) / (T2 - T200) x 100, with Tr read as the thickness recovered to at 2 kPa.
daulta_varshney_2021_200kPa.derivation: From the two definitions, T200 / T2 = (TR - CR) / (1 - CR). So these carpets compress by 42-68 % of their 2 kPa thickness at 200 kPa; the 14 mm, least dense pile (S3) compresses most.
daulta_varshney_2021_200kPa.note: The paper does not print T2 or T200 themselves; the derived ratio depends on reading Tr as a thickness.

vuruskan_2017_dynamic_loss.note: Mean thickness loss after 50-1000 dynamic impacts (Table 5), i.e. wear, not compression under load. Used only as support that taller pile deforms more.

hirai_gunji_2001.order: carpets A, B, C, D, E, F, G (Table 1), machine (tufting) direction, static coefficient as reported

oy_pull_slip_meter.method: O-Y pull slip meter (JIS A 5705-1992 appendix method). Load 785 N on a slider of 8 cm x 7 cm = 56 cm2 (about 140 kPa, derived), pulled at 18 deg and 785 N/s.
oy_pull_slip_meter.sole_note: Table 3 labels the rubber-type sole 'PVC'; the text calls it the synthetic-rubber outsole, Shore A73 (leather A94).

jsma_slip_meter.method: JSMA (Japan Shoe Manufacturers Association) slip meter. Men's business shoe with an SBR outsole (sole A83, heel A78), 700 N vertical load, 2 m/min, toe to heel.
jsma_slip_meter.note: Reported as a static coefficient although the sole moves at 2 m/min; no separate kinetic value is given.

inclined_plane.method: Shimadzu inclined plane (type 1P-T), men's shoe on dry carpet, extra loads 0, 10, 20, 30 N.
inclined_plane.note: The authors found no significant load dependence (within +-0.09 between 0 and 30 N).

hirai_gunji_2001.findings: Leather is more slippery than synthetic rubber; cut pile gives more friction than loop pile on the inclined plane; friction is higher across the tufting direction than along it (only along-direction values are tabulated).

brandao_2017.method: Static coefficient from the maximum pull of a force gauge on the WABIAN-2 humanoid foot loaded with 1.5 kg. Rigid foot, sole covered with a high-stiffness soft material and an anti-slippage sheet. 5 measurements per surface, at least 3 surfaces per material.
brandao_2017.note: Very light normal load (about 15 N on a full-size humanoid foot), far below this robot's pad pressure.

friction.kinetic: No kinetic (sliding) coefficient for rubber, TPU or silicone soles on carpet was found.
friction.tpu_silicone: No measured friction of TPU or silicone soles on carpet was found.

us_access_board_2003.note: Wheelchair rolling, 'a limited study'; wheels, not a toe dragging through pile. Context only: pile resists motion more as it gets taller.

rolling_resistance.toe_drag: No sourced coefficient for a toe or claw moving through carpet pile was found.

pr662_measured_in_model.note: Outputs of the robot_floor surrogates on PR #662's 9.9 kg model, not measurements of carpet.

singh_2024.value: MuJoCo foot-geom solref time constant randomized uniformly in (0.02, 0.4) s, resampled about every 0.5 s; one ablation fixes 0.4 s. Surfaces: 'blue mattress', 'block of soft cushion foam', 'soft gym mattress'. No solimp, stiffness, damping or sink depth reported; range 'chosen by trial and error and visual inspection'.
singh_2024.note: Soft terrain for a full-size humanoid, not carpet.

simulation_contact.carpet_specific: No published carpet contact stiffness or damping used in robot simulation was found.

screening_values.note: What designlab/carpet.py uses. Each value names its basis: sourced, derived (rule stated) or assumption.

low.basis_height: sourced: top of the low band (homedit_2023)
low.basis_compression: derived: largest 98 kPa compression as a fraction of pile length among the six Hirai and Gunji carpets with pile 6.5 mm or less (carpet G, 4.0 mm loop pile)

medium.basis_height: sourced: top of the medium band (homedit_2023, flooringclarity_2025)
medium.basis_compression: derived: Hirai and Gunji carpet E (7.0 mm cut-pile rug, non-woven backing), the most compressible sample

high.basis_height: sourced: top of the high band (homedit_2023, flooringclarity_2025)
high.basis_compression: assumption: no compression at foot pressure was found for pile above 7 mm, so the medium value is carried over. Taller pile compresses more (daulta_varshney_2021: up to 68 % of total thickness at 200 kPa for 14 mm pile; vuruskan_2017), so this may understate high-pile sinkage; the module also reports the fully compressed bound

reference_pressure_kPa.basis: sourced (hirai_gunji_2001 initial load; ISO 1765 thickness is read at 2 kPa)

carpet_friction_band.basis: sourced: range of every rubber-type sole value in hirai_gunji_2001 Table 3 (O-Y PVC dry and wet, JSMA SBR dry and wet, inclined plane 0-30 N); leather excluded. brandao_2017 carpet 0.82 +- 0.02 falls inside

carpet_friction_foot_pressure.basis: sourced: hirai_gunji_2001 O-Y meter, PVC/synthetic-rubber sole at about 140 kPa, dry and wet

hard_floor_friction.basis_model: the compiled MJCF: floor and pad defaults (0.9), combined by MuJoCo's element-wise maximum; not sourced
hard_floor_friction.basis_robot_foot_band: sourced: brandao_2017 ceramic, marble and wood, mean +- one standard deviation

contact_impedance_d0.basis: assumption (numerical, not sourced): a constant impedance (d_0 = d_w) makes every pile contact a linear spring whose static stiffness is set by its solref, whatever d is. 0.5 rather than MuJoCo's default 0.9 because MuJoCo's contact regularisation adds an inertia of d / ((1 - d) A) per contact: about 1/A (0.6-0.9 kg) at 0.5, against 5-8 kg at 0.9. With the several hundred probe contacts of the pile floor, d = 0.9 added 1.5-4 t of contact-space inertia and the servo-held stance rocked heel to toe at about 2.5 Hz without settling (60-M-T-10, low pile, 12 s).

contact_damping_ratio.basis: assumption: MuJoCo's constraint-space damping ratio (solref dampratio), not a physical damping ratio; no sourced carpet damping was found (robot_floor's carpet uses 1.2). Only the static stiffness of the pile floor is matched to a source.

torsional_rolling_m.basis: robot_floor carpet values, kept as the repository's starting point; not sourced

gaps: No carpet damping (loss factor or rebound) usable for a contact model was found; the damping ratio is an assumption.
No compression at foot-like pressure for pile above 7 mm; high-pile compression is carried over from a 7 mm rug.
Only end points of the compression curve (2 and 98 kPa; 2 and 200-220 kPa) were found, not its shape, so the floor model is linear.
The 98 kPa compression was held 5 min on a presser foot of about 1 cm2; a 0.5-0.7 s stance on 3-8 cm2 pads may compress less.
No kinetic friction and no TPU or silicone sole data on carpet were found.
No sourced resistance for a toe dragging through pile; wheelchair rolling data are context only.
No published carpet stiffness or damping for robot simulation was found; robot_floor's values are unsourced.
